name: Enoxaparin
high_alert_note: ISMP's 2024 acute-care high-alert list includes antithrombotic agents, explicitly low-molecular-weight heparin anticoagulants such as enoxaparin. This does not authorize unit-for-unit conversion or replace prescribed dosing and local neuraxial/bleeding safeguards. Classification is independently cited in the evidence report; medication content retains its registered FDA/manufacturer sources without the restricted ISMP material.
summary: Low molecular weight heparin for prophylaxis of deep vein thrombosis in surgical and medical patients and other labelled indications (the label read is a subcutaneous product). The boxed warning covers spinal and epidural haematomas with neuraxial anaesthesia or spinal puncture. Nursing focus: bleeding, platelets, neuraxial procedures and renal function, HIT risk, platelet trends, neuraxial precautions and avoidance of unit-for-unit substitution.
evidence_type_note: The evidence here is a regulator product label (prescribing information written for prescribers and pharmacists). It is not a bedside nursing practice guideline: the nursing actions are inferences from label warnings, marked partial, and the unit's protocol governs practice. A targeted 2026-11-21 cross-check used the May 2026 DailyMed Lovenox branded label for unit-for-unit interchangeability, renal considerations, HIT contraindications and monitoring; this does not replace the original label record or pharmacist approval.
jurisdiction_note: US FDA label only. EMA, MHRA and SFDA labels were not read; indications, warnings and presentations differ by country and by manufacturer.

items.text: The label describes enoxaparin as a low molecular weight heparin indicated for prophylaxis of deep vein thrombosis in abdominal, hip and knee replacement surgery and in medical patients, and for other thrombotic indications.
Monitor for bleeding and platelet changes, and check for any planned or recent spinal or epidural procedure before each dose.

Review recent renal function, weight and clinical indication before administration; when renal clearance is reduced or a neuraxial catheter/procedure is planned, verify the order and timing with the responsible clinician/pharmacist rather than applying an unreviewed generic regimen.
Monitoring frequency and alarm limits follow the unit's protocol for this medicine.
The label calls for frequent monitoring for signs of neurological impairment and for signs of bleeding.

The current US Lovenox label recommends monitoring complete blood count (including platelets), occult blood where ordered and clinical signs of bleeding. Anti-factor Xa testing may be considered by the treating team in renal impairment or selected safety concerns; PT and aPTT are not adequate measures of enoxaparin's anticoagulant effect. The team decides if, when and how these tests guide care.
Boxed warning: epidural or spinal haematomas may occur in patients anticoagulated with low molecular weight heparins who are receiving neuraxial anaesthesia or undergoing spinal puncture.
Monitor for signs of bleeding, and for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with or without thrombosis; monitor the platelet count closely.

Enoxaparin is not interchangeable unit-for-unit with unfractionated heparin or other low-molecular-weight heparins. They have different prescribing and dosing requirements; any change of anticoagulant requires an authorized new order and the appropriate transition/monitoring protocol, not a direct numerical substitution.
Women with mechanical prosthetic heart valves who are pregnant may be at increased risk of thrombosis.

In severe renal impairment, the current US branded enoxaparin label requires indication-specific prescriber dose adjustment because exposure and bleeding risk can rise. Review renal function and obtain a pharmacy/prescriber check of the existing order; this educational draft does not supply dosing thresholds or regimens.

Active major bleeding and a history of immune-mediated heparin-induced thrombocytopenia within the past 100 days or persistent HIT antibodies are contraindications in the current US branded label; check prior HIT and new platelet trends and escalate suspected HIT rather than assuming every fall in platelets confirms it.
The label lists spinal or epidural haematoma and increased risk of haemorrhage among the serious adverse reactions.

The label also identifies thrombocytopenia as a serious adverse reaction. Common reactions in the label include anaemia, bruising, injection-site pain and increased aminotransferases; occurrence depends on the indication and study population.

Postmarketing reports include thrombocytopenia with thrombosis, skin necrosis and systemic allergic reactions including anaphylactic or anaphylactoid shock. These voluntary reports do not reliably establish frequency or causality.
Hyperkalaemia has been reported after marketing, often with other predisposing factors such as renal dysfunction or potassium-raising medicines.
Report new back pain, leg weakness or numbness, bowel or bladder change, any bleeding or a falling platelet count immediately.

Use the unit's early warning score (for example, the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2 track-and-trigger system) to standardise recognition of acute deterioration: a medium aggregate score is a key trigger for an urgent clinical review, and a high aggregate score triggers an emergency clinical response. This is a generic nursing escalation framework, not specific to this medicine; it does not replace this medicine's own escalation triggers, which remain local protocol.
Record the product and order checks, monitoring results, adverse events and escalation per unit standard.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Check neuraxial anaesthesia or spinal puncture history around each dose.
Watch for bleeding at any site.
Review the platelet count as ordered.
Report neurological change in the legs or bleeding at once.

Review ordered CBC/platelet trends, renal function and bleeding assessments; do not treat PT/aPTT as reliable measures of enoxaparin effect. Anti-Xa testing, if indicated, is clinician/pharmacist-directed.

gaps: Renal impairment and selective anti-Xa monitoring are now discussed at safety-awareness level based on current US branded labeling, without dosing or lab targets; local indication-specific prescribing, renal dosing and anti-Xa interpretation still require pharmacist review. Reversal remains outside this draft.
The label read is the subcutaneous route; intravenous use for other indications is not summarised.
